items.stem: Which term describes the process by which the ownership of media is held by fewer and fewer companies?
items.answer: Concentration of ownership
items.markingKey: Concentration of ownership: the process by which the ownership of media is held by fewer and fewer companies. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “diversification”, and give one example.
items.answer: When a media company expands into different types of media or other industries. Example: a TV company buying a football club.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (when a media company expands into different types of media or other industries); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a TV company buying a football club. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “synergy” and “diversification”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Synergy: the cross-promotion of a product across the different media owned by one company (e.g. a film promoted through the owner’s TV channels, music and games). Diversification: when a media company expands into different types of media or other industries (e.g. a TV company buying a football club).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A global entertainment corporation releases a film, then promotes it through its own TV channels, sells the soundtrack on its music label and launches a video game through its games division. Suggest how a neo-Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Neo-Marxism: media content reflects ideological hegemony: journalists from similar backgrounds share middle-class, pro-establishment assumptions, so dominant values appear as common sense (Glasgow University Media Group, Hall).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A global entertainment corporation releases a film, then promotes it through its own TV channels, sells the soundtrack on its music label and launches a video game through its games division. Explain how a radical feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Radical feminism: the media are part of patriarchal culture: they objectify women, present male dominance as normal and serve men’s interests (Mulvey, Wolf).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A global entertainment corporation releases a film, then promotes it through its own TV channels, sells the soundtrack on its music label and launches a video game through its games division. Compare how interactionist and neo-Marxist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Interactionism: media help construct social reality and labels; audiences interpret messages actively, and media reactions can amplify deviance (Cohen, Young). Neo-Marxism: media content reflects ideological hegemony: journalists from similar backgrounds share middle-class, pro-establishment assumptions, so dominant values appear as common sense (Glasgow University Media Group, Hall).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful self-completion questionnaires are for studying how far news content differs between newspapers owned by the same company.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee. Limitations: response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative; closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how far news content differs between newspapers owned by the same company but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful case studies are for studying the views of journalists working for large media companies.
items.answer: Strengths: a single case can give rare insight into an unusual or closed group; they may use several methods, increasing validity. Limitations: the researcher’s interpretation may be biased; one case may be untypical, so findings cannot be generalised. Theory: case studies are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce mainly qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the views of journalists working for large media companies but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.answer: Concentration of ownership
items.markingKey: Concentration of ownership: the process by which the ownership of media is held by fewer and fewer companies. [1]

items.answer: When a media company expands into different types of media or other industries.

items.stem: Distinguish between “media conglomerate” and “vertical integration”.
items.answer: Media conglomerate: a large company that owns many different types of media and often other businesses. Vertical integration: when a media company owns all stages of production, distribution and sale.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: Yusuf, a sociology student, is designing a project on the views of journalists working for large media companies. Explain one strength of using field experiments for this research.
items.answer: They take place in a natural setting, so behaviour is more realistic than in a laboratory.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the views of journalists working for large media companies. [2]

items.stem: A research team is investigating how far news content differs between newspapers owned by the same company. Explain one strength and one limitation of using content analysis for this study.
items.answer: Strength: quantitative content analysis using a coding sheet can be repeated by another researcher, so it is reliable. Limitation: coding categories reflect the researcher’s own interpretation, so different coders may disagree.
items.markingKey: For each: 1 mark identified; 1 mark explained in the context of how far news content differs between newspapers owned by the same company. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes the view that owners directly use the media as tools to spread ruling-class ideology?
items.answer: Instrumental Marxism
items.markingKey: Instrumental Marxism: the view that owners directly use the media as tools to spread ruling-class ideology. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “ideological state apparatus”? Give one example.
items.answer: Althusser’s term for institutions such as the media that spread ruling-class ideology. Example: TV and newspapers promoting consumerism.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (Althusser’s term for institutions such as the media that spread ruling-class ideology); 1 mark for a relevant example such as TV and newspapers promoting consumerism. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “instrumental Marxism” and “hegemony”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Instrumental Marxism: the view that owners directly use the media as tools to spread ruling-class ideology (e.g. a proprietor telling editors which party to support). Hegemony: Gramsci’s term for the dominance of ruling-class ideas achieved through consent rather than force (e.g. audiences accepting that free markets are “common sense”).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A newspaper owner in Lagos appoints a new editor who shares his views; within a year the paper stops criticising the government’s tax policy. Suggest how a pluralist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Pluralism: power in society is spread between many competing groups; the media are diverse, respond to audience demand and reflect a range of views, so no single group controls them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A newspaper owner in Manila appoints a new editor who shares his views; within a year the paper stops criticising the government’s tax policy. Explain how pluralist and Marxist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Pluralism: power in society is spread between many competing groups; the media are diverse, respond to audience demand and reflect a range of views, so no single group controls them. Marxism: the media are owned and controlled by a capitalist class who use them to spread ruling-class ideology, creating false consciousness and protecting capitalism (Miliband, Murdock and Golding).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using official statistics to research how television news reports industrial disputes.
items.answer: Strengths: they give national data on whole populations that no single researcher could collect; they are collected regularly, so trends over time and comparisons between groups can be made. Limitations: they are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs; they show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how television news reports industrial disputes but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of self-completion questionnaires for studying how journalists decide what to report.
items.answer: Strengths: there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee; closed, pre-coded questions produce quantitative data that is easy to compare and turn into statistics. Limitations: pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences; respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how journalists decide what to report but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.answer: Gramsci’s term for the dominance of ruling-class ideas achieved through consent rather than force.

items.stem: Miliband argued that the media are used by the capitalist class to legitimate capitalism and divert attention from inequality. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Miliband argued owners use the media to create false consciousness and present capitalism as natural. Criticism: Journalists have professional independence; owners rarely intervene directly.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Marxism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Omar is planning a study of how television news reports industrial disputes. Explain one strength of using structured interviews for this research.

items.stem: A newspaper owner in Bangkok appoints a new editor who shares his views; within a year the paper stops criticising the government’s tax policy. Explain how postmodernist and Marxist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: media-saturated society offers endless choice; audiences actively construct identities from media images, and reality and representation blur (Baudrillard, Strinati). Marxism: the media are owned and controlled by a capitalist class who use them to spread ruling-class ideology, creating false consciousness and protecting capitalism (Miliband, Murdock and Golding).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Source A: “A content analysis of 120 television news reports about strikes in Kathmandu found that managers were interviewed in 70% of reports and strikers in 35%. Words such as “demands” and “threats” were used for unions, while managers “offered” and “proposed”.” Use Source A and your own knowledge to answer the questions. (a) Using Source A, explain one strength of the method used for studying bias in news reporting. (b) Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that the news media are biased in favour of the powerful.
items.answer: (a) Quantitative content analysis using a coding sheet can be repeated by another researcher, so it is reliable. (b) For: The source shows unequal access and loaded language; GUMG and Hall argue news reflects dominant ideology. Against: Pluralists argue news reflects news values and audience demand; content analysis cannot show intentions or audience effects; coding is open to researcher bias; other reports may differ. Also consider how far a single study using content analysis can support a general claim. Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for a relevant strength; 1 mark for applying it to the study in the source. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple points from the source or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): explained points for and against using the source and own knowledge. Level 3 (5-6): balanced, well-supported evaluation with comment on the evidence and a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “public service broadcasting”? Give one example.
items.answer: Broadcasting funded by the public and required to inform, educate and entertain all sections of society. Example: a licence-fee-funded national broadcaster.

items.stem: Explain the difference between “consumer sovereignty” and “regulation”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Consumer sovereignty: the idea that audiences’ choices determine what the media produce (e.g. programmes with low ratings being cancelled). Regulation: rules set by governments or independent bodies to control media content and ownership (e.g. a regulator requiring balance in TV news).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful self-completion questionnaires are for studying the range of political views in national newspapers.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised. Limitations: closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity; they measure what people say they do, not what they actually do. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the range of political views in national newspapers but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: The table shows the share of newspaper circulation held by the three largest companies in a country near Dubai. Table: share of national newspaper circulation (%) | 2000 | 2022. Company A | 24% | 32%. Company B | 18% | 22%. Company C | 14% | 11%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Company C between 2000 and 2022. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that media ownership is becoming more concentrated.
items.answer: (a) 11 − 14 = -3 percentage points. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Company A, Company B; the figure fell for Company C; Company A had the highest figure for 2022. Mergers and takeovers (horizontal integration). Qualifications: Print circulation is falling; online news offers many alternative sources; ownership share does not prove control over content. The data also come from official statistics of 3 newspapers in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 14 and 11; 1 mark for -3 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using structured interviews to research how far news content differs between newspapers owned by the same company.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; response rates are usually higher than for postal questionnaires because the interviewer is present. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. items.stem: A survey of 240 adults in Lagos asked where they got their news. Table: adults using each source for news in the last week (%) | 2013 | 2023. Television | 75% | 62%. Social media | 20% | 43%. Print newspapers | 41% | 17%. (a) Calculate the gap between Social media and Print newspapers in 2013 and in 2023, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that audiences now have more choice, as pluralists argue.
items.answer: (a) 2013: 21 percentage points; 2023: 26 percentage points; the gap widened. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Social media; the figure fell for Television, Print newspapers; Television had the highest figure for 2023. Young people prefer social media. Qualifications: Social media news may come from the same large organisations; algorithms limit what people see; choice of source is not the same as diversity of views. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 240 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.

items.stem: Industry figures on newspaper circulation are shown below. Table: share of national newspaper circulation (%) | 2000 | 2022. Company A | 24% | 36%. Company B | 19% | 22%. Company C | 16% | 16%. (a) Using the data, identify the group with the highest figure for 2022. (b) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Company A between 2000 and 2022.
items.answer: (a) Company A (36%). (b) 36 − 24 = +12 percentage points.
items.markingKey: (a) Company A, 36%. [1] (b) 1 mark for using 24 and 36; 1 mark for +12 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2]

items.stem: A single company in Colombo owns two national newspapers, a television channel, a radio network and the country’s most popular news website. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: the media are owned and controlled by a capitalist class who use them to spread ruling-class ideology, creating false consciousness and protecting capitalism (Miliband, Murdock and Golding).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Omar is planning a study of how far news content differs between newspapers owned by the same company. Evaluate the use of content analysis for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: it allows representations to be compared over time or between different media; quantitative content analysis using a coding sheet can be repeated by another researcher, so it is reliable. Limitations: coding categories reflect the researcher’s own interpretation, so different coders may disagree; it shows what content contains but not how audiences interpret it. Theory: content analysis is favoured by positivist (quantitative content analysis) or interpretivist (qualitative content analysis) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how far news content differs between newspapers owned by the same company but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using official statistics to research how far news content differs between newspapers owned by the same company.
items.answer: Strengths: they give national data on whole populations that no single researcher could collect; they are collected regularly, so trends over time and comparisons between groups can be made. Limitations: they show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them; definitions and methods of collection may change over time, making comparisons difficult. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how far news content differs between newspapers owned by the same company but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Which term describes the view that economic factors such as profit and advertising shape media content?
items.answer: Political economy approach
items.markingKey: Political economy approach: the view that economic factors such as profit and advertising shape media content. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “bias”.
items.answer: A one-sided or distorted presentation of events.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a one-sided or distorted presentation of events. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): hegemony means rule by force alone. Reason (R): journalists from similar backgrounds share establishment values. Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
items.answer: A is false but R is true
items.markingKey: A is false: “hegemony means rule by force alone.” is incorrect; R is a true statement. [1]

items.stem: Study the following extract (Source A) from a report on research carried out in Doha. “A content analysis of 120 television news reports about strikes in Hanoi found that managers were interviewed in 70% of reports and strikers in 35%. Words such as “demands” and “threats” were used for unions, while managers “offered” and “proposed”.” (a) Using Source A, identify two findings of the study. (b) Explain one limitation of the method used in Source A for studying bias in news reporting.
items.answer: (a) 1. Managers were interviewed twice as often as strikers. 2. Language presented unions as aggressive and managers as reasonable. (b) Counting images or words may miss their deeper meaning and context.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each finding taken from the source. [2] (b) 1 mark for a relevant limitation; 1 mark for applying it to the study in the source. [2]

items.stem: A newspaper owner in Dhaka appoints a new editor who shares his views; within a year the paper stops criticising the government’s tax policy. Suggest how a pluralist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Pluralism: power in society is spread between many competing groups; the media are diverse, respond to audience demand and reflect a range of views, so no single group controls them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: During a dock strike in Cape Town, most news reports interview managers in their offices and show queues of lorries, while strikers are filmed shouting at the gates. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: the media are owned and controlled by a capitalist class who use them to spread ruling-class ideology, creating false consciousness and protecting capitalism (Miliband, Murdock and Golding).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Read Source A. “A content analysis of 120 television news reports about strikes in Cairo found that managers were interviewed in 70% of reports and strikers in 35%. Words such as “demands” and “threats” were used for unions, while managers “offered” and “proposed”.” (a) Identify the main research method used in the study described in Source A. (b) Using Source A, explain one strength of the method used for studying bias in news reporting. (c) Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that the news media are biased in favour of the powerful.
items.answer: (a) Content analysis. (b) It allows representations to be compared over time or between different media. (c) For: The source shows unequal access and loaded language; GUMG and Hall argue news reflects dominant ideology. Against: Pluralists argue news reflects news values and audience demand; content analysis cannot show intentions or audience effects; coding is open to researcher bias; other reports may differ. Also consider how far a single study using content analysis can support a general claim. Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) Content analysis. [1] (b) 1 mark for a relevant strength; 1 mark for applying it to the study in the source. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple points from the source or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): explained points for and against using the source and own knowledge. Level 3 (5-6): balanced, well-supported evaluation with comment on the evidence and a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the idea that audiences’ choices determine what the media produce?
items.answer: Consumer sovereignty
items.markingKey: Consumer sovereignty: the idea that audiences’ choices determine what the media produce. [1]

items.stem: Briefly explain Compaine’s view that the media market remains competitive and diverse.
items.answer: Compaine argued the internet and new entrants prevent any single company from dominating.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the idea; 1 mark for developing it: Compaine argued the internet and new entrants prevent any single company from dominating. [2]

items.stem: Explain Curran’s argument that there is little evidence of owners directly controlling content, but commercial pressures narrow diversity, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Curran found owners intervened at times, but pressures of profit and advertising were more important. Criticism: Pluralists argue his evidence of intervention is limited to a few cases.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Neo-Marxism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: A TV channel in Lisbon cancels an expensive drama after poor ratings and replaces it with a cheaper reality show that attracts younger viewers. Suggest how a neo-Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Neo-Marxism: media content reflects ideological hegemony: journalists from similar backgrounds share middle-class, pro-establishment assumptions, so dominant values appear as common sense (Glasgow University Media Group, Hall).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Explain two features of the pluralist view of the media.
items.answer: Diversity and competition; consumer sovereignty; professional journalism; regulation and public service broadcasting; power spread between groups.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): one or two simple points, limited sociological knowledge. Level 2 (4-6): explained points using some concepts, studies or theories. Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: Diversity and competition; consumer sovereignty; professional journalism; regulation and public service broadcasting; power spread between groups. [8]
